en: Regarding the phrase "because it is a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatvāt*), he now states the purpose of the qualification "present" (*idānīntanatva*) applied to the "effort" (*kṛti*) that constitutes the property of being achievable by present effort, which is included by the word "etc. (*ādi*)—this is expressed in the words "therefore, [it is] future" (*tena bhāvī*). He states the purpose of that same qualification when applied to the "desire" (*icchā*) that constitutes the property of being a means to what is desired—this is expressed in the words "likewise, [one who is] satiated" (*evaṃ tṛptaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "extremely undesirable" (*balavadaniṣṭa*):

He states the purpose of that qualification in the case of strong aversion: "and it proceeds," etc. "In the proceeding" means prior to the actual proceeding. "From the knowledge of being a means to hell" means from the knowledge of being a means to a strong undesirable result in the form of hell. "By intense attachment and so forth."
The meaning is: "by means of intense passion (*rāga*) and so forth toward the pleasure of approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamanādi*). Regarding the word "hell" (*naraka*):

it means "a powerful undesirable [consequence]. Regarding "due to concealment" (*tirodhānāt*): it means "due to non-arising. The underlying sense is that even if there exists intense passion for such pleasure, because of the presence of a powerful aversion (*dveṣa*) toward the hell produced by approaching those who should not be approached, [the passion does not manifest].

Regarding the phrase "having the form of activity" (*pravṛtirūpā*): the meaning is that in the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), effort (*kṛti*) enters [into the definition] by way of its nature as activity (*pravṛtitvena*). Even in the system of the author of the *Maṇi* (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi), who maintains that the cause [of action] is the cognition of being achievable through an effort dependent on one's own desire (*svecchādhīnakṛtisādhyatājñāna*), the state of being dependent on one's own desire (*svecchādhīnatva*) is a qualification of the effort.

The meaning is that [the desire] is for the sake of attaining the performance whose nature is activity (*pravṛtti*). And in this way, the desire which has become its operation should also be understood as having "being achievable through activity" as its qualifier (*prakāra*), because there is a cause-and-effect relationship between knowledge and desire based on their having the same qualifier. By that, [it is meant] by means of the entry of activity.
[Objection: There is no activity [of the body] when there is movement of the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that because the vital breaths are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), there is no perception of their material cause, and thus there is no resulting activity whose accomplishment depends on the movement of the vital breaths having those breaths as its material cause; for [if that were so], there would result an activity whose accomplishment depends on the movement of the vital breaths having as their material cause the channels through which the vital breaths flow.
This must be stated:

for it is precisely in order to prevent the occurrence of an activity that is accomplished by the movement of breaths initiated by the taking up of a vehicle in a village that the status of the knowledge of being achievable through activity is accepted as a cause [of action]. Even though...

Although the prevention of such activity is possible simply by accepting that the knowledge of "being achievable through effort" is the cause [of activity] via the relation of being the qualificand of a specific obstruction to the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃcāra*), nevertheless, in order to prevent the occurrence of activity toward objects such as a jar due to the error that it is achievable through the effort of the life-force (*jīvanayoni-yatna*), [the following is stated].

It should be understood that it is necessary for the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*pravṛtisādhyatvajñāna*) to be the cause [of activity]. By this, the following objection is refuted: "Even if the knowledge of being achievable through effort is the cause in order to prevent activity regarding the movement of breath (*prāṇasaṃcāra*), the occurrence of activity regarding the movement of breath would still be unavoidable due to an error (*bhrama*) concerning its being achievable through effort."

Nor should it be argued that, even if the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*pravṛtti-sādhyatā-jñāna*) is a cause [of action], it would be unavoidable for an action to arise toward the fatigue that is invariably concomitant with eating, as that too is achievable through effort; for no such action arises precisely because there is an absence of desire to act (*cikīrṣā-viraha*) regarding such fatigue. And the absence of desire to act in that case is due to...

Because exertion is of the nature of suffering, the knowledge of its being suffering acts as an obstacle to desire; thus, it is simply due to the absence of the general causal complex for desire that [effort] does not arise.

By this, [it is shown that] the knowledge of being achievable by an effort subject to one's own will is required to prevent the contingency of engaging in exertion that is not incidental [to another goal].

The view of the author of the *Maṇi* that "causality must be stated" is refuted. Nor should it be argued that, since there is knowledge of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*) and desire regarding pleasure, there would follow the occurrence of an inclination (*pravṛtti*) toward it through the relation of the objective state called "being an object-to-be-accomplished"; for [this is not the case] by way of being an object-to-be-accomplished.
Because the cognition of something being a fruit with respect to an activity acts as an obstacle [to that activity]. In reality, however,

since it has been established in various places that the difference from a particular property (tat-tad-dharma-bheda) is the cause for a cognition with respect to a subject-locus (viṣayatā) that does not reside in that particular property, and in that context, within the scope of the determinant of the effect-ness (kāryatāvacchedaka)...
In place of "jñānatva" (cognitiveness), "guṇatva" (quality-ness) itself should be inserted. And thus,

with respect to the relation of being an object residing in something other than pleasure-ness, quality-ness is that which delimits the state of being produced by the cognition of being achievable through effort.

Since the distinction between the pleasure that generates [an action] and the pleasure itself— qualified by that [distinction]— is absent from pleasure (sukhatva) due to its being the pervader of the state of being an activity (*pravṛttitva*) related to the objective domain called "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhyatā*), there is no occurrence of activity in that [pleasure] as the delimiting factor of the objective domain called "that which is to be accomplished. This is because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates [an effect] is delimited by a property that is pervaded [by the property of being an activity].

Since the causal complex delimited by a pervading property is required for the production of an effect, it should be understood that, by this very method, activity is prevented in the case of breath-movement and fatigue with respect to their being objects characterized by the relation of being the delimitor of the objective state known as "probandum" (sādhyatā).

Keeping this very point in mind, the Miśras have stated that there is no activity toward that [state] precisely because the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is unfit for such activity; this is the general direction. "And thus" means:
and in the case where the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth is the cause of activity.

By the phrase "because it is a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatvāt*) and so forth, there is the inclusion of [the properties of] being not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) and being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). And here, because there is no engagement with that which is fruitless, [the property of] being a means to what is desired [is required]; and even in the case of something that is a means to what is desired...
Since one does not engage in eating food mixed with honey and poison, nor in actions that are achievable only through great effort but lack a powerful desirable result—

such as the lifting of Mount Sumeru— it follows that the knowledge of [an action's] being achievable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and its being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence is the cause of engagement. And since this knowledge arises from an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the injunctive suffix is the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth.

This is the intended meaning. Now, an objection is raised: in order to prevent activity toward future events such as the status of crown prince (*yauvarājya*), it must be stated that the knowledge of being achievable by one's current effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) and so forth is the motivator;
yet that [knowledge] cannot be derived from an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*). Therefore...

Since a cognition characterized by the mode "being accomplished through human effort" and "being a means to a desired end" alone arises, how can it be said that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the instigator of action? To this, they reply:
the injunction does not directly produce the instigating cognition; rather, from the injunctive sentence and so forth, [the cognition of] being a means to a desired end [arises].

Once it is understood that [an action] is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛtisādhya*), the inquiry arises as to "what is desired? In response to this, through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), there arises—either inferential or mental—the cognition that [the action] is a means to heaven; otherwise, [it could not be known] in its specific form.

Because activity is impossible in the absence of knowledge of the result, the knowledge that [the action] is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and so forth, including its being present-time (*idānīntanatva*), arises from inference. For this very reason, the author of the *Maṇi* also stated: "The knowledge produced by the knowledge generated by an injunction (*vidhi*) is the motivator. In this regard:

The Bhaṭṭapādas [state]: In the world, activity (*pravṛtti*) is of two kinds: that which is dependent on one's own will and that which is produced by the instigation of another. Although it is of no use for instigating the former, it is the motivator (*prayojikā*) for the second kind of activity, as seen in common usage such as "I am doing this because of the teacher's instigation. And this instigation (*pravartanā*)...
The "causing to proceed" (*pravartana*) is a specific activity conducive to engagement;

this is, for a conscious being, simply the intention (*abhiprāya*), whereas for the insentient Veda, it is a certain [activity] called denotation (*abhidhāna*) inherent in the word. Thus, through the knowledge of the teacher’s intention, the disciple [proceeds].

In the same way, activity proceeds from the knowledge of the denotation in the case of an injunction; that [denotation] alone is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and that alone is called the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) by virtue of its being the optative element, whereas the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) is expressed by virtue of its being the verbal inflection element (*ākhyātatva*). Thus it has been said: "They say that the optative suffixes and the like express a quite different [productive energy], namely the verbal productive energy (*abhidhābhāvanā*)."

"But the other, the efficient-force (bhāvanā) directed toward the object, is the domain of all verbal suffixes. Here, *abhidhā* means "word"; the efficient-force residing in that [word] is "verbal-efficient-force" (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*). The "object" (*artha*) is either the sacrifice or the self; "being the object" (*arthātmakatva*) means having the object as its domain or being dependent upon the object. Thus, it has the sacrifice and so forth as its domain, and is dependent upon the self.

The *pravṛtti* (activity) is the *arthabhāvanā* (the efficient force toward the object). In this context, it should be understood that the *arthabhāvanā* alone is the objective (*bhāvya*) of the *śabdabhāvanā* (the verbal efficient force), and the fruit of the *arthabhāvanā* is heaven and so forth. As it has been said: "In the optative suffix (*liṅ*), there is an expression; that itself is the *śabdabhāvanā*, and its objective is the activity of the person."
"The cognition of the relationship is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the incitement (*prarocanā*) is employed as its auxiliary (*aṅga*).

This is the meaning: the denotation (*abhidhā*) is the expressed meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). When there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to what its result (*bhāvya*) might be, it is stated that "the [injunction] is its result. When there is an expectancy as to by what means it is to be brought about...

Regarding "saṃbandhabodhe": the cognition of the relation is the knowledge of the word-potency (śakti) residing in words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*). In that regard, they say: "Since a person might desist due to indolence, praise (*stuti*) incites him; therefore, it is an auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)," which is expressed by the term *prarocanā*. That is not correct, because in the world, activity is dependent upon one's own will.

Since the cognition of a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) has already been established as the cause [of action], let that alone be the cause even in other instances of engagement; what is the use of postulating a separate cause in the form of a cognition of an instigation (*pravartanā*)? For this very reason, even in the case of the Veda, the cognition of an instigation is not the cause, because there exists a function called *abhidhā* (denotation) which is distinct from the word's power (*śakti*).

And because there is a lack of evidence [for any other such factor]. For this very reason, Maṇḍana Miśra stated in his *Mīmāṃsānukramaṇī*: "For men, there is no other motivator toward actions than the fact that they are means to a desired end; and they declare that 'incitement' (*pravartanā*) is the property which is the cause of engagement.
By this, he has expressed that "incitement" is simply the state of being a means to a desired end, insofar as it is conducive to engagement.

[Objection: But in this case, in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," since no fruit is heard and there is thus an absence of the cognition that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), there would be no inclination to act;
therefore, he says: "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*). This means: and when being a means to a desired end and so forth is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*). [Objection: But...

With the intention that, since there is no fruit in obligatory rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is not the motivator, nor is that its object the meaning of an injunction, he raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*). And [he says] "nor is it based on an explanatory passage" (*nacārthavādikaṃ*):
"Those who perform the twilight worship... (*sandhyām upāsate ye tu*)...

The meaning is that this is established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Those whose vows are constantly praised, having shaken off their sins, go to the eternal world of Brahman. [The opponent objects: "Because it would result in the loss of its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). This implies the conviction that there is a contradiction between being obligatory (*nitya*) and being optional (*kāmya*). [The author replies: "But there is no evidence for a contradiction between those two," as seen in such scriptural injunctions as "One should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) every day. Saṃdhyām upāsate...

Thus, by the force of the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between these two meaningful [texts], a combined qualification (*saṃvalitādhikāra*) is postulated for one who desires the fruit obtainable at that time; therefore, he says: "in the absence of desire.

"Because of the consequence of non-performance" means because of the consequence that no transgression (*pratyavāya*) would arise from its non-performance. This refers to the non-performance by one who lacks qualification due to the absence of the qualification consisting of desire.

The sense is that there is an absence of being a generator of demerit (*pratyavāya*). Now, one might object: "Even so, the scriptural mention of a fruit in the context of obligatory rites (*nitya*) would still be purposeless. Anticipating this doubt, he says—"And thus"—intending to show that its purport lies merely in praise by way of being an *arthavāda*. The phrase "from the assumption" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Even though the desire presented by the *arthavāda* constitutes the qualification (*adhikāra*), because [the text]— in such passages as "one who does not perform the enjoined action"— teaches that the non-performance of what is enjoined produces demerit (*pratyavāya*) when there is purity (*śauca*), [this applies] to one whose [non-performance] is conjoined with such a desire.

Purity and the like do not constitute the qualification (*adhikāra*); rather, in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), it is the desire for the fruit that constitutes the qualification. Thus, there is no conjunction between purity and the desire for the fruit as two qualifications; consequently, even in the absence of desire, since the qualification consisting of purity and so forth exists, the non-performance of the *saṃdhyā* and other such rites at that time necessarily produces demerit (*pratyavāya*). This remains true even if one maintains that desire itself is the qualification.

For one who possesses that qualification but lacks purity and so forth, the status of being a generator of demerit (*pratyavāya*) for the non-performance of the *saṃdhyā* and other rites is not postulated; rather, the status of being a generator of demerit for non-performance is postulated even for one who possesses only a portion of the qualification— namely, purity and living at that time— even though the qualification is not fully conjoined.

It should also be understood that this is because of the absence of desire for the earth [as a result]. By this, it is indicated that there is no deficiency even if there is no evidence for the presence of a desire for the fruit as a rule in that case. Now, one might object:
"In the activity directed toward obligatory rites (*nitya*), the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is indeed the cause."

To the objection—"If [the action] is already established by this very [fact], for what purpose should one postulate that even an obligatory (*nitya*) act is also optional (*kāmya*)?"—he replies: "No, it is not so. [The reason is that] it is the state of being a means to one's own desired end (*sveṣṭasādhanatva*). The sense is that, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), knowledge of something being a means to a desired end is the cause of activity delimited by [the occurrence of] inclination (*pravṛtti*).

For this very reason, in the *Kusumāñjali*, having raised the objection that the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is performed even though it is fruitless because it is enjoined by the Veda, the teachers [Udayana] disregarded it by stating that "this is the view of a certain teacher (Guru), not the view of the Guru [Gautama]. And as for the unseen merit (*apūrva*)...

He refutes the Prābhākara position that the purpose of obligatory (*nitya*) action is intrinsic by stating "yadapi" ("as for that which..."). "In the absence of desire" means in the absence of desire for a result consisting of *puṇya* (merit) or *apūrva* (unseen potency). "By the logic of the Rātrisatra" means as follows: For example: [text continues]

When there is a desire to know the fruit of those rites produced by sentences such as "Jyotis," "Gauḥ," and so forth—which are denoted by the term *rātrisatra*—it would be cumbersome to postulate a heaven or other results that are not at all heard in the text; therefore, by way of an exception to the *Viśvajit* principle, [the text states]:
"Those who perform these [rites] indeed become firmly established."

In the case of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "approaching the nights," it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the fruit is indeed "firm standing" (*pratiṣṭhā*); likewise here too, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the fruit is simply the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) mentioned in the explanatory passage. Otherwise, there would be an absence of a fruit. Therefore, one should assume a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage.
For the sake of brevity, he demonstrates the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passages (arthavāda) in various places, beginning with the words "non-arising" and so forth.

"Precisely for this reason" means: precisely because the satisfaction of the ancestors is the fruit of the *śrāddha* rite. Regarding the term "general rule" (*utsarga*): if the fruit of the *śrāddha* and other rites were to reside in the agent alone, then since there would be no deviation [from that outcome], it would indeed be a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

The sense is: "It might be so. Even if one accepts the *apūrva* (unseen potency), he states that it is not possible for the knowledge of its being a means to be the motivator: "For the sake of the *apūrva*" and "nor is it a means to that. And thus, because it lacks the status of a fruit due to the absence of being an object of desire (*icchā*), [it cannot be a motivator].

The cognition of that [action] as a means to that [result] is the motivator; this is the future [point]. Now, even in your view, since there is no arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*), how can it be a result? Consequently, it would lack the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Nor could it be an object of desire on the grounds of being a means to the human goal consisting in the non-arising of suffering.

Anticipating the objection that the non-arising of suffering—which consists of antecedent non-existence—is not produced by [the performance of a prohibited act], he refutes it with the words beginning "pratyavāya" (transgression). In the phrase "anutpattau," the locative case signifies the state of being the subject of the proposition.
How can there be activity? [This is because] the non-arising of transgression occurs according to the manner previously described.

The meaning is: since the knowledge that something is a means [to a goal] is not a cause for activity when it lacks the status of being a fruit, how can there be activity toward such things as the *saṃdhyāvandana*? "Absence of transgression" (*pratyavāyābhāva*) refers to the prior non-existence of transgression (*pratyavāya-prāgabhāva*). "In its absence" means in the absence of obligatory rites (*nitya*) such as the *saṃdhyāvandana*.

The absence of that [is] the absence of the absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*). In the absence of that, i.e., in the absence of the absence of transgression, the absence of that [is] the absence of the prior non-existence of suffering (*duḥkhaprāgabhāva*), which is of the nature of suffering itself. Regarding the phrase "common to acquisition and preservation" (*yogakṣemasādhāraṇā*): acquisition (*yoga*) is the obtaining of what has not yet been obtained.

Acquisition (*prāpti*) is the preservation of what has been attained; this is because, in the causal role of the cognition that something is a means to a desired end toward activity, it is precisely the "means-ness" common to both [the attainment of what was not yet acquired] and "preservation" (*kṣema*) that enters into the definition. This is the intended meaning. [This is so] because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is swallowed up by the dilemma regarding its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

The moderns, however, maintain that because the production of a fruit is impossible [in the case of a mandatory rite], the absolute non-existence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) alone is the fruit of the obligatory (*nitya*) act; for while there is the absolute non-existence of being produced by a commonality consisting of *yoga* (acquisition) and *kṣema* (preservation) characterized by a specific connection with one's own nature, [the fruit] exists. It is exactly thus that it is common to both *yoga* and *kṣema*. Now, [one might object] regarding the [prohibition] "one should not eat *kalañja*": [...]* *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical argument concerning the nature of the fruit of obligatory rites and the definition of *yogakṣema-sādhāraṇa* as presented in the fragment.)*

Since there is no obstacle to accepting the understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that "the absence of eating *kalañja* is a means to what is desired," he asks: "How can the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) be connected with the meaning of an injunction?

That is to say, how can there be a connection between the meaning of an injunction and the meaning of the negative particle—the absence—which is itself connected to such things as being a means to what is desired?

The meaning is: "How can there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the case of eating *kalañja*? [The answer is] "Because it is impossible"; the implication is that such a connection is sublated (*bādhāt*) in the act of eating *kalañja*. [Regarding the phrase] "merely the state of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence":

this refers to the fact that since the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) is accepted as having its denotative power (*śakti*) in all three—being achievable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), etc.—in some cases, one or another of these may be absent.

The sense is that in some cases, the cognition of a certain injunctive meaning is accepted [as the cause]. Regarding inclination (*pravṛtti*), there is the causality of a single [cognition] characterized by being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), qualified by being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and qualified by not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), due to parsimony (*lāghava*); however, it is not [the causality] of cognitions whose objects are each of these individually, such as being achievable through effort and so forth.
Out of respect for this rule, it is possible that the denotable meaning must indeed be qualified;

and thus, in a context of negation, the absence of the qualified [object] is conveyed by the *nañ* associated with the injunction—this is the intention behind saying "or else. [The phrase] "it rests upon the absence of the qualifier" [is explained as follows].

The point is this: when the absence of a qualified property (*viśiṣṭābhāva*)—namely, the absence of being a means to a desired end and so forth—is understood with respect to such acts as eating *kalañja* (poisoned meat), it results in the absence of the qualification of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvābhāva*). If the qualified [property] were the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*), then how [could there be an injunction] regarding the *śyena* sacrifice, given that the qualification consisting in "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" is sublated (*bādha*) in that case?
He raises the objection that there is a comprehension of a qualified injunctive meaning: "But [in the case of] the *śyena*...

Here, *śyena* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). "One practicing sorcery" (*abhicaran*) means desiring the killing of an enemy. [The question] "How? [is asked] because its [the literal meaning of the word *śyena*] is sublated in that context; such is the sense. This is the meaning.
"It is the object of a cognition produced by an injunction; because it is enjoined, it is not prohibited"—this is the meaning.

The point is that, in accordance with the slaughter of animals for sacrifice, the prohibition "one should not kill" refers to violence other than that which is enjoined. Regarding "malevolent magic" (*abhicāra*): likewise, [it is said] "malevolent magic and the *ahīna* sacrifice [are purified] by three [days]."

The sense is that, since it would follow that the instruction on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would be rendered useless if [the prohibition] were otherwise, it is impossible for the prohibitory injunction to have a scope other than that [specific act]. Nor does this imply that even the killing of an animal for sacrifice would result in the production of demerit (*pratyavāya*).

It must be stated that the prohibitive injunction "one should not harm" (mā hiṃsyāt) pertains to acts of harming other than those for which no specific expiation has been prescribed. For indeed, only an action conducive to death is "harming" (hiṃsā), and since the Śyena sacrifice is not of that nature, it does not fall within the scope of the prohibition "one should not harm. Thus, [the distinction] certainly exists.

With the intention that [an action] must not be followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, he states the fault in the view that any activity whatsoever conducive to death—whether direct or indirect—is *hiṃsā* (harming), saying: "If any activity whatsoever conducive to death were *hiṃsā*, then... [directly].
The meaning is that if every activity whatsoever, even one common to ordinary tradition, were considered violence (*hiṃsā*), then [the definition would be too broad].

Now, if the inclusion of "having death as the objective" (*maraṇoddeśyakatva*) is required, then in a case where a Brāhmaṇa dies from an iron arrow (*nārāca*) discharged with a different intention, there would be no expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because that [act] would lack the status of violence. Therefore—
Since it is not the object of the prohibition "one should not kill," he says: "having another as its objective.
Regarding the term "scriptural": the meaning is that it is not [prohibited] by virtue of being the object of the prohibition "one should not kill.

Regarding the phrase "by way of not having the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as an intermediary": this is because the Śyena sacrifice brings about the death of the enemy solely through the intermediary of the unseen.
[The opponent] says: "Let it be that the hawk [sacrifice] is an act of violence (*hiṃsā*);

what is the purpose of the qualification 'not having the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its mediating factor'? To this he replies: "For this very reason. This means: precisely because of the qualification "not having the unseen merit as its mediating factor. [He concludes: "It is not an act of violence. And thus...

The point is that by the necessary qualification "not mediated by the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," which serves to exclude such acts as the worship of Śiva, the nature of the Śyena sacrifice as violence is also excluded. Now, one might object:
if the exclusion of such worship of Śiva and the Śyena sacrifice is achieved simply by the qualification "directly producing death," [then what is the need for the other?]

The bystander raises an objection as to why the qualification "not mediated by the unseen" (*adṛṣṭādvārakatva*) is necessary for the Guru: "Nor [is it so] directly," etc. He states the view of those who maintain that the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) can be established in the case of the Śyena sacrifice even without the qualification of not being mediated by the unseen: "But some," etc. [Regarding] violence (*hiṃsā*).
"Result" (phala) means that the operation which directly brings about death is the result; [this refers] to that [operation], such as the striking with a sword.

"The state of being a producer of sin" [is established] because it is understood from the passage beginning with "that which is not performed by one who is impure or deficient" (*abhicārimahīnaṃ ca*) that malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) produces sin.

The point is that the very operation which directly causes death is the meaning of the term *abhicāra*. Nor should it be argued that this is redundant because the idea that only an operation which directly causes death constitutes *hiṃsā* was already raised previously by the words "not... etc."; for what was previously [addressed] was the [operation] which directly causes death.

For while it was suspected here that the *apūrva* produced by the Śyena sacrifice possesses the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*), [the same is not suspected] of sword-strokes and the like, which are of such a nature; thus there is a distinction. Nor, according to this view, does the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) include the *apūrva* produced by the Śyena as an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) toward the sword-stroke itself.

Because it lacks the quality of being a direct cause of death. Nor should it be argued that if violence (*hiṃsā*) were defined as an operation that directly causes death, then the case of a Brāhmaṇa who dies from a series of wound-infections following a sword-strike would remain inexplicable as an instance of violence; for in that case, [the causal process] occurs immediately after the sword-strike itself.

Since death occurs through the arising of defects such as the *sannipāta* [disorder], that [the act of killing] functions as an instrument (*vyāpāra*) toward it; and because there can be no intervention by an instrument [in this case], why then do the followers of the Āstika schools not engage in the *śyena* sacrifice? To this he says: "The subsequent... and so forth. Thus, because it is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of sin, it is not [permissible].

The sense here is that this is the motivation for those who hold the view that [the sacrifice] exists. On this point, the moderns (navya) argue as follows: although the hawk [sacrifice] falls within the scope of the prohibition "one should not kill," it is nonetheless universally agreed that it generates sin because it is a malevolent rite (abhicāra), since Manu has included malevolent rites among the minor sins (upapātaka).

How can it be that this [the Śyena sacrifice] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence? As for the claim that it is only the sword-strike and so forth produced by the Śyena that constitutes the *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) and thus generates sin, while the Śyena itself does not—this too is incorrect, because of the word *abhicāra* in the passage beginning with "the *abhicāra*, the *mahāvrata*, and... [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.2.10].

Otherwise, because the hawk and other such [animals] that produce that [death] would not be included, there would be no expiation in cases where, despite the recognition [of the animal as the same], death does not result from a sword-stroke or similar means. Even so, in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice, since it is the instigator of sin, it is precisely the knowledge that it does not instigate a powerful undesirable [consequence] that serves as its cause.
Because it is precisely that object which constitutes the meaning of the injunction; and thus, having established that the *śyena* sacrifice is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence,
[the injunction] pertains to killing as being achievable through an effort characterized by being a means to a desired end qualified by not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.

However, it is not logical that there is a single potency; rather, having accepted a triad of potencies, one must admit that in some cases there is the cognition of a certain meaning, and in other cases the cognition of another. But in instances such as "by means of the Śyena sacrifice," there is simply no cognition of the property of being unaccompanied by a more powerful undesirable consequence (balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva).

[The word "only" (eva) is used] to restrict [the denotation] to the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). Furthermore, it is not logical to assume a single power (*śakti*) in the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa*) due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. Nor is there a lack of a regulating principle when one accepts powers for each [constituent] and admits the cognition of a particular meaning in certain cases.

This must be stated: since it is *tātparya* (intention) alone that is the restrictive factor, even under the view that there is a separate power (*śakti*) for each word, there is no contingency of sentences such as "one should go to a woman who should not be approached" (*agamyāṃ gacchet*) being authoritative by virtue of generating a valid cognition of their being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). This is because [such a result] is not desired. As for the conventional designation of them as non-authoritative in that case, [it is due to the speaker's intention].
Sometimes [the cognition] is based on the generation of an error regarding the fact that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.

Nor is it the case that the cognition is only "the cooking is achievable through effort (kṛtisādhya) while being a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhana) and not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence," and not in the form "while being achievable through effort... and so forth.
It should not be argued that even on the view that there is a single power for the qualified [complex], there is a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*);
for the fact that the cognition occurs only in that way and not otherwise is something to be determined by *śapatha* (an oath).

Therefore, the first alternative is that there is a distinct power for each of the components, such as "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) and so forth.
It is thus [properly] qualified. Even there, "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" is not the intended meaning;
for even the pain that is an unavoidable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) of sacrifices and the like may, at some time or other, become an object of powerful aversion for someone or another.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence that injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would lack authority; and furthermore, there would be the consequence that prohibitions such as "one should not sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice" (*na aśvamedhena yajeta*)—just like prohibitive injunctions such as "one should not eat *kalañja*"—would also possess authority. [This is because] whenever a person engages in the horse-sacrifice and similar acts...
The claim that the meaning is "the state of not being a producer of an object of a strong cognition belonging to that person at that time" is not correct;
for it would involve the conceptual complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a distinct injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) for every difference in time and person,
and because it is impossible to specifically identify particular times and particular persons, [the definition] cannot include those specific times and persons.

Furthermore, because [the capacity] is difficult to grasp, there would result the lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) for prohibitive injunctions such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," just as there is for prohibitive injunctions such as "One should not sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). In that case,
[the definition of the object of desire must be] the state of not being the producer of an object of intense aversion belonging to that person at that time.
Even in that case, because [the action] exists, however, the meaning of a Vedic injunction is the non-production of demerit (*adharma*);

it is precisely the absence of that [demerit] which is conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*) in such statements as "one should not eat *kalañja*. For the sake of maintaining the validity of sentences such as "one should not eat vegetables," the meaning is also the non-production of disease.

In the same way, in such cases as "one should not marry during the Puṣya asterism" or "one should not climb a mountain alone," it should be understood that the meaning is the production of various undesirable results. Nor does this entail an infinity of potencies,
such as those corresponding to hellish states, diseases, and so forth.

They argue that this is because one accepts a single denotative power (*ekaśakti*) over the aggregate of absences whose counter-correlates are delimited by various [properties], having unified them through the delimitors of the object-domain of aversion (*dveṣaviṣayatāvacchedakatva*), which serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*);
or else, because one accepts a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the worldly optative suffix (*liṅ*) in cases such as "not being a producer of disease" and so forth.
The meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is the intention of a reliable person (*āpta*), and that [intention] implies that [the action] is a means to achieve what is desired by oneself;
furthermore, the knowledge that something is a means to achieve what is desired is the motivator—thus he states the view of the teacher Udayana with the words "But the teacher...
and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth," the inclusion of the first-person form "I should cook" (*pākaṃ kuryām*) is intended.

By the phrase "command and so forth," the inclusion of "request" and the like is intended. Thus, it is established that in the second and first persons—such as in "you should cook" (pākaṃ kuryāḥ) and "I should cook" (pākaṃ kuryām)—the verbal suffixes express desire in the form of command and request; by analogy with these examples, it can be inferred that even in the third person, the suffixes express desire.

The state [of being]. "Due to parsimony" (lāghavāt) means that, in view of the potency of the injunction as desire (*icchātva*), there is parsimony compared to [the potency of] being a means to a desired end not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhīṣṭasādhanatva*), and so forth. This is the meaning; this is the cognition. "By inference" (*anumāya*)...

In this context, the following inference should be noted: "The sacrifice is a means for me, who desires heaven, to achieve a desired end that is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, because it is intended by a trustworthy person as something to be accomplished by my effort, just like my own meal which is intended by me as something to be accomplished by my effort."

Because of the absence of that [author], there is an absence of being desired by a trustworthy person (āpta), and consequently, there is an absence of the knowledge that [the act] is a means to achieve a desired end, which is caused by that [desire].
Now, since there is no speaker in the Veda, whose desire is to be conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*)?
To this he says: "But he who... and "The injunction itself (*vidhi*). This means that in conveying a desire distinct from that of a speaker, it is the injunction [that functions].

The sense is that, due to the absence of such capacity [on the part of humans], the Veda itself is the means of valid cognition regarding the Lord as its speaker. And as for the "non-remembrance of an author": this refers to the non-remembrance—that is, the lack of mention—in the Smṛtis of an author, namely, the author of the Veda. Thus, the Veda is not of human origin (apauruṣeya).
The meaning is that the inference "because its author is not remembered" constitutes a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). [This refers to the arguments of] Kapila, Kaṇāda, and so forth.
